pages.text:
*The Bearer's Almanac, Entry 5: A river builds the land it will one day drown.*

The causeway was a thin scar of packed earth cutting through the delta’s expanse. It smelled of dried reeds and old brine, a scent that stuck to the back of the throat and lingered. The mud on either side had cracked into perfect hexagons. The pattern repeated endlessly until the eye ached from trying to count the tiles.

Wen walked in the middle of the path. Her boots sank slightly with each step. To her left, a row of stranded fishing boats lay on their sides. Their hulls were exposed to the sun, bleached and dry. To her right, the dry bed of the river stretched out. It was a vast, pale desert where water had once rushed with a roar she could feel in her teeth.

Master Gao walked ahead of her. His polished black boots clicked rhythmically on the packed earth. He held a leather-bound ledger under one arm and gestured broadly with the other. He looked like he was presenting a painting in a gallery.

"Look at this," he said. His voice carried that smooth, practiced charm that had made the villagers trust him too easily. He stopped and pointed to the cracked mud. "This is not just dirt. This is the river’s own skin. Every year, the Clear River carries silt from the mountains, fine as flour, and deposits it here. A thousand years of that, Wen Lan. A thousand years of patience."

Wen frowned, looking down at the hexagons. "It looks dead."

"Dead?" Gao laughed. It was a short, bright sound. "No, my dear. It is waiting." He tapped the ledger against his thigh. "The river builds the land it will one day drown. It is a very patient landlord." He looked back at her, his smile sharp and precise. "And right now, the landlord is holding the rent."

Wen felt a cold prickle at the base of her skull. The words sounded reasonable. Almost poetic. But there was a hardness to them that did not fit the gentle landscape. She looked at the stranded boats. The masts pointed accusingly at the sky. The silence pressed in.

pages.text:
They found Shen Yu on the edge of the dry channel. He knelt in the dust, a surveyor’s staff planted firmly beside him. Pale skin, almost translucent in the harsh light, framed a head of short black hair that stuck up in places, as if he had been running his hands through it in frustration. A brown canvas vest covered a white shirt with cuffs stained dark blue with ink. Round brass-rimmed glasses caught the sun.

He did not look up when Gao approached. He adjusted a red flag stuck in the ground next to his staff.

"Three meters," he muttered to the flag, not the men. "Down to the bone. The water table dropped three meters in a week."

Wen stopped a few paces away. "Is that bad?"

Shen Yu looked up. He blinked, seemingly surprised to see other humans.

"Bad?" He straightened. His glasses slid down his nose. "Bad is losing a shoe. This is losing the floor." He wiped his hands on his vest, leaving dark ink streaks on the brown fabric. "I am measuring the fall. If the river is three meters lower, the pressure is gone. The silt settles. The channel dies."

Gao placed a hand on Shen Yu’s shoulder. The gesture felt practiced. "We are all measuring the fall, young man. But some of us are looking for the cause."

Shen Yu pulled his shoulder away. His jaw tightened. "Causes are for philosophers. I work in numbers." He picked up his rolled map case and clutched it to his chest like a shield. "If you are going upriver, you are walking into a place that does not want to be walked into. The math says so."

Wen looked at the red flag. A small, defiant spot of color in the grey dust. "Do you have a map of the channel?"

Shen Yu hesitated. Then he unrolled a corner of the map case. The paper was thick, covered in fine lines and numbers. "I do. But it is not a map of where to go. It is a map of where you should not."
pages.image: Shen Yu kneeling in dusty mud, adjusting a red flag next to a surveyor's staff, wearing a brown vest and round glasses, Wen Lan and Master Gao standing nearby, dry riverbed and cracked earth in the background.

pages.text:
Shen Yu talked quickly, his words tumbling over each other like stones in a dry creek bed. He unrolled the map on a flat rock and tapped a line with a finger stained blue with ink.

"See this slope?" he said, pointing to a gentle curve on the paper. "The river used to flow at one degree. Now, with the water level down, the effective slope has changed. When water slows, it drops its silt. That silt builds up the bed. The bed gets higher. The channel gets shallower. The water slows more. It is a loop. A trap."

Wen watched the line of his finger. "So the river is burying itself?"

"Essentially, yes." Shen Yu adjusted his glasses, pushing them back up his nose. "It is a self-sealing wound. Without intervention, the channel will close within a month. The delta will become a plain. The boats will stay here forever, becoming monuments to a mistake."

Gao leaned in, his expression unreadable. "A mistake made by whom?"

Shen Yu looked at Gao, then at Wen, then back at the map. His voice dropped. "By the water itself, if you are looking for a villain. But there are... irregularities in the silt distribution. Pockets of high density where there should be low density. It is as if something is filtering the flow. Selectively."

Wen felt a chill that had nothing to do with the wind. "Filtering?"

"A weir," Shen Yu said, the word crisp and hard. "But not a natural one. A constructed one. Upstream. Far upstream." He rolled up the map with a snap. "I am not supposed to discuss this. My master, the surveyor, has orders to keep the data local. But you are walking upriver. You will find the weir before you find the answer."

Gao smiled, a thin, precise line. "Then we had better walk quickly."
pages.image: Shen Yu pointing at a detailed map on a rock, Wen Lan and Master Gao leaning in to look, the map covered in lines and numbers, a dry riverbed stretching behind them, sunlight glinting off Shen Yu's glasses.

pages.text:
Wen turned to Gao, the question still hovering between them like a bird that had not yet decided whether to land. "Is it true? Is there something upstream stopping the river?"

Gao did not answer immediately. He looked at Shen Yu, then out at the vast, cracked expanse of the delta, and for a moment the easy charm drained from his voice, replaced by a careful, measured stillness.

"Shen Yu is an apprentice," Gao said finally, his tone smooth as polished jade. "He measures. He does not decide. There are many reasons a river can slow. Drought. Heat. The earth itself is tired."

"Three meters," Shen Yu interjected, his voice tight and brittle. "In a week. That is not tiredness. That is a valve."

Wen looked at Gao. "You know."

Gao’s smile did not waver, but his eyes did. They were dark, deep, and utterly still, like the bottom of a well that has seen no rain for a decade. "I know that the river is a complex system, Wen Lan. And I know that you are young, and afraid, and that fear makes one see patterns in the chaos." He closed the ledger under his arm with a soft thud. "But if you wish to find the source, you will need a guide who knows the path. I can offer you that. Shen Yu can offer you numbers. Which do you choose?"

Wen looked at Shen Yu. He was staring at the ground, his hands trembling slightly against the edge of the map case. "I am not a guide," he said quietly. "I am a witness. And I have seen the weir. I have seen the stones. They are not natural."

Gao’s expression hardened, the charm cracking to reveal the steel beneath. "Then you have seen something that should remain unseen."

Shen Yu looked up, his eyes fierce behind his brass-rimmed glasses. "I am coming with you. If there is a weir, I need to measure it. If the river is being held, I need to know how much it is costing."

Gao studied him for a long moment, the silence stretching thin and taut like a tracker's rope before a haul. Then he nodded, a slow, deliberate motion. "Very well. We all have our debts to pay."
pages.image: Wen Lan looking intently at Master Gao, who is smiling thinly, Shen Yu standing beside her with a determined expression, the dry delta and stranded boats in the background, a tense atmosphere.

pages.text:
The sun began to dip below the horizon, painting the sky in shades of bruised purple and burnt orange. They reached the edge of the delta where the land ended abruptly, giving way to a sea of mist that rolled in from the valley beyond. It was thick and white and silent, pressing against the dry air like a heavy curtain.

Wen stood at the precipice, her boots planted firmly on the cracked earth. Before her stretched the dry riverbed, a vast, pale road that wound its way into the mist, disappearing into the unknown. It was a path of dust and memory, a ribbon of silt that had once carried life to the sea. The texture was rough and granular under her feet, the kind of grit that stuck to the soles of her cloth-wrapped boots and ground between her teeth when she spoke.

She looked at the road, and for the first time, she did not feel fear. She felt a strange, cold clarity. The river was not gone. It was waiting. And she was going to wake it up. The thought settled in her chest with the quiet certainty of a stone sinking into still water. There was no hesitation in it, only the steady pull of a current she could not yet see but knew to be there.

Gao stood beside her, his silhouette sharp against the fading light. "It is a long way to the source," he said softly. "The mist will hide the path. The cold will test your resolve. And the river... the river will test your heart."

Wen looked at Shen Yu, who was adjusting his glasses, his hands finally steady. He wiped a smudge of dust from the brass rims with his sleeve, a meticulous gesture that seemed out of place in the wild expanse around them. "I am ready," she said.

The wind picked up, carrying the scent of dust and distant rain. It ruffled the blue cloth in her ponytail and stirred the loose threads of her grey sash. Wen took a deep breath, and then another, filling her lungs with the dry air. She turned to face the mist, and took the first step onto the dry road.
